question: What is statistical learning, how do we estimate f and measure model accuracy, and why does flexibility trade bias against variance?
contributions: Defines the model Y = f(X) + eps and the prediction versus inference goals.
Contrasts parametric and non-parametric estimation, and flexibility versus interpretability.
Introduces training versus test MSE, the U-shaped test error, and the bias-variance decomposition.
Introduces the classification setting: error rate, Bayes classifier, Bayes error rate, KNN.
Python lab (numpy, pandas, matplotlib basics) and 10 exercises.

results.claim: Expected squared prediction error splits into a reducible part and the irreducible variance of the error term (fixed f-hat and X).
results.setup: Y = f(X) + eps, eps independent of X with mean zero; f-hat and X held fixed so only eps varies.

results.claim: Expected test MSE at x0 decomposes into variance of f-hat(x0), squared bias of f-hat(x0), and Var(eps); it can never lie below Var(eps).
results.setup: Averaged over many training sets drawn from the same population, tested at x0. Proof stated to be beyond the book's scope.

results.claim: On the simulated two-class data, the KNN classifier with K=10 gets a test error rate close to the Bayes error rate.
results.setup: Simulated 2-D data of Fig 2.13 (100 observations per class in the plotted sample), KNN K=10, Bayes error as baseline.
results.quote: The test error rate using KNN is 0.1363, which is close to the Bayes error rate of 0.1304.
results.note: The text also prints the Bayes error rate for this same simulated data as 0.133 (p. 36). 0.133 and 0.1304 are inconsistent as printed.

results.claim: KNN with K=1 overfits and K=100 underfits on the same data; neither predicts well.
results.setup: Same simulated data as Fig 2.13, KNN K=1 and K=100 (Fig 2.16). Baseline is the Bayes error rate quoted on p. 37.
results.quote: they have test error rates of 0.1695 and 0.1925, respectively.

results.claim: Bayes error rate on the simulated two-class data is above zero because the classes overlap.
results.setup: Simulated data of Fig 2.13, conditional probabilities known from the generating process.
results.quote: For our simulated data, the Bayes error rate is 0.133.
results.note: Same quantity printed as 0.1304 on p. 37.

results.claim: KNN training error is 0 at K=1; the KNN test error is U-shaped in 1/K with a minimum near K=10.
results.setup: Fig 2.17: training set of 200 observations, test set of 5,000 observations, same data as Fig 2.13, 1/K on log scale. Curves are jumpy because the training set is small.
results.quote: the test error exhibits a characteristic U-shape, declining at first (with a minimum at approximately K = 10)

results.claim: Linear regression has two degrees of freedom, the most restrictive end of the flexibility axis in Fig 2.9.
results.metric: degrees of freedom of linear fit
results.setup: Fig 2.9: simulated data, linear regression versus smoothing splines of increasing flexibility.
results.quote: linear regression is at the most restrictive end, with two degrees of freedom.

results.claim: Training MSE falls monotonically with flexibility while test MSE is U-shaped; the best flexibility depends on how linear the truth is (Figs 2.9 to 2.11).
results.setup: Three simulated data sets: moderately non-linear f (Fig 2.9), near-linear f (Fig 2.10), highly non-linear f (Fig 2.11). Test MSE computed on a very large test set because f is known.
results.note: Exact MSE values are not in the text; only read from plots.

results.claim: Overfitting is defined as small training MSE with large test MSE, specifically when a less flexible model would give a smaller test MSE; training MSE is almost always below test MSE even without overfitting.
results.quote: Overfitting refers specifically to the case in which a less flexible model would have yielded a smaller test MSE.

results.claim: A rough thin-plate spline fits the 30 Income observations with zero training error but is far more variable than the true f.
results.metric: training errors of rough spline fit
results.setup: Simulated Income data, 30 individuals, two predictors (years of education, seniority), thin-plate spline with low smoothness (Fig 2.6).
results.quote: This fit makes zero errors on the training data.

Lab shows numpy variance divides by n, not n-1, by default.
results.setup: rng = np.random.default_rng(3); y = rng.standard_normal(10); np.var(y) equals np.mean((y - y.mean())**2) = 2.72.

limits: The bias-variance decomposition (Eq 2.7) and the Bayes classifier optimality are stated without proof.
All MSE and error-rate curves are from simulated data; no real-data test MSE is reported in the chapter text, and exact curve values are only in figures.
The Bayes error rate for the simulated data is printed as 0.133 on p. 36 and 0.1304 on p. 37.
Semi-supervised learning is mentioned and declared out of scope.
Lab code uses delim_whitespace=True in pd.read_csv, which pandas has since deprecated (use sep=r'\s+'); np.random.default_rng outputs may differ across numpy versions, as the authors warn.
Cross-validation as the way to estimate test MSE is deferred to Chapter 5.
practices: Choose the method by test MSE (or test error rate), not training MSE, because training error falls with flexibility regardless of fit to new data (Sec 2.2.1).
When no test set exists, estimate test MSE from the training data with cross-validation (Sec 2.2.1, Ch. 5).

Prefer inflexible, interpretable models such as linear regression or the lasso when inference is the goal; use flexible ones when only prediction matters, but a less flexible method can still predict better (Sec 2.1.3).
Always keep the bias-variance trade-off in mind, even though bias and variance cannot be computed when f is unknown (Sec 2.2.2).
Treat the Bayes classifier and Bayes error rate as the unattainable gold standard and irreducible-error analogue for classification (Sec 2.2.3).
Choose K in KNN by test error; K=1 gives low bias and high variance, large K gives high bias and low variance (Sec 2.2.3).
Choose regression versus classification by whether the response is quantitative or qualitative; predictor type matters less provided qualitative predictors are coded (Sec 2.1.5).
Set a random seed with np.random.default_rng(seed) for reproducible results (Lab 2.3.3).
Mark missing values with na_values when reading data, then drop or handle them explicitly (Lab 2.3.7).
No one method dominates over all data sets (no free lunch), so selecting the method per data set is a core task (Sec 2.2).

terms.definition: error introduced by eps, which cannot be predicted using X, so no estimate of f removes it; Var(eps) bounds the achievable accuracy
error from f-hat being an imperfect estimate of f, which can be reduced by a better learning technique
a two-step approach: assume a functional form for f, then fit its parameters (e.g. least squares for a linear model)
methods that make no explicit assumption about the functional form of f and need many more observations
a method yields a small training MSE but a large test MSE because it follows noise too closely
MSE = (1/n) sum (y_i - f-hat(x_i))^2 computed on the data used to fit the model (Eq 2.5)
Ave(y0 - f-hat(x0))^2 over previously unseen test observations (Eq 2.6)
the amount by which f-hat would change if estimated using a different training data set
the error introduced by approximating a real-life problem by a much simpler model
good test performance needs low variance and low squared bias; extremely low bias is easy with high variance and vice versa
a quantity that summarizes the flexibility of a curve
(1/n) sum I(y_i != y_hat_i), the proportion of mistakes on the training observations (Eq 2.8)
assigns each observation to the class j with largest Pr(Y=j | X=x0); minimises the test error rate on average
1 - E(max_j Pr(Y=j | X)), the lowest possible test error rate, analogous to the irreducible error (Eq 2.11)
estimates Pr(Y=j | X=x0) as the fraction of the K nearest training points N0 with y_i = j (Eq 2.12) and classifies to the largest
responses y_i exist for all observations / for none (clustering) / for only m of n observations

figures.caption: Left: Data simulated from f, shown in black. Three estimates of f are shown: the linear regression line (orange curve), and two smoothing spline fits (blue and green curves). Right: Training MSE (grey curve), test MSE (red curve), and minimum possible test MSE over all methods (dashed line).
figures.why: Shows the monotone training MSE and U-shaped test MSE at once, with the Var(eps) floor.

figures.caption: Details are as in Figure 2.9, using a different true f that is much closer to linear.
figures.why: Near-linear truth: linear fit beats the flexible fit.

figures.caption: Details are as in Figure 2.9, using a different f that is far from linear.
figures.why: Highly non-linear truth: flexibility pays; best flexibility depends on f.

figures.caption: Squared bias (blue curve), variance (orange curve), Var(eps) (dashed line), and test MSE (red curve) for the three data sets in Figures 2.9-2.11.
figures.why: The clearest picture of Eq 2.7 and the bias-variance trade-off in three regimes.

figures.caption: A representation of the tradeoff between flexibility and interpretability, using different statistical learning methods.
figures.why: Orders subset selection, lasso, least squares, GAMs, trees, bagging/boosting, SVMs, deep learning by flexibility versus interpretability.

figures.caption: A simulated data set consisting of 100 observations in each of two groups ... The purple dashed line represents the Bayes decision boundary.
figures.why: Defines the Bayes decision boundary on a concrete 2-D example.

figures.caption: The KNN approach, using K = 3, is illustrated in a simple situation with six blue observations and six orange observations.
figures.why: Step-by-step KNN vote (2 blue, 1 orange) and the resulting boundary.

figures.caption: A comparison of the KNN decision boundaries obtained using K = 1 and K = 100 on the data from Figure 2.13.
figures.why: Jagged versus near-linear boundary shows variance versus bias in K.

figures.caption: The KNN training error rate (blue, 200 observations) and test error rate (orange, 5,000 observations) on the data from Figure 2.13, as the level of flexibility (assessed using 1/K on the log scale) increases.
figures.why: Classification analogue of the U-shaped test curve, with Bayes error as floor.

figures.caption: Linear fit, smooth thin-plate spline, and rough thin-plate spline on the Income data.
figures.why: Underfit, good fit and overfit of the same 30 points side by side (pp. 21-23).

figures.caption: A clustering data set involving three groups ... Left: well-separated. Right: some overlap.
